161698041.title: File:-mypubliclandsroadtrip 2016- Get outdoors Baby, King Range National Conservation Area (28487604443).jpg

ObjectName.value: -mypubliclandsroadtrip 2016- Get outdoors Baby, King Range National Conservation Area (28487604443)

Categories.value: PD US BLM|Male toddlers|United States photographs taken on 2016-08-20|Flickr images reviewed by FlickreviewR 2|Standing toddlers|U.S. Bureau of Land Management Flickr files uploaded by OptimusPrimeBot|King Range National Conservation Area|Walking children seen from behind

ImageDescription.value:
From our family to yours – mom and BLMer Rachel Sowards Thompson shares one of her family favorites on #mypubliclandsroadtrip!

“As a mother, I love weekends hiking or camping in the King Range National Conservation Area with my boys (ages 1 ½ and 3 ½). We also love to bring along our neighbors girls (ages 8 and 12) to add some extra adventure. The kids enjoy exploring the Bear Creek Nature Trail and playing games in their Junior Explorer activity book (available at the King Range Project Office along with the Hidden Valley Quest brochure) - great way to look for and identify new creepy crawlers in the creek.

Our favorite spot to pitch our tent and of course, roast s'mores at night is the Wailaki Campground, located along U.S. 101 to Redway, west 22 miles on Briceland/Shelter Cove Road, south 2 miles on Chemise Mountain Road. This Campground has facilities: 13 tent/trailer campsites with picnic tables, fire rings and vault toilets. There’s plenty of potable water, which make great “wa-wa” puddles for toddlers. There are no hookups for trailers. We have met so many wonderful families here over the years and as an employee for the Bureau of Land Management, it is fun to see visitors enjoying their public lands. Also, one more thing to mention, Wailaki is also wheelchair accessible.

There are trails to and from the campgrounds that lead 1.5 miles up to the top of Chemise Mountain or families can enjoy the newly developed quest in Hidden Valley that's only a couple miles down the road. The 2 mile loop trail provides beautiful views of the ocean and passes through a historic apple orchard. If you finish the quest, be sure to pick up your patch at the King Range Project Office. The Bear Creek Nature Trail is 0.5 miles between Wailaki and Nadelos Campgrounds. There are interpretive panels about Native American uses of the land along with phenology monitoring panels and notebooks for parents and kids to fill out to help the BLM monitor the seasonal changes of plants. Cross the boardwalk and find yourself on the west side of Bear Creek and a great spot for the Bear Creek Critters activity. West of the creek is a trail that twists and turns 1.5 miles to the top of Chemise Mountain where families will be rewarded with awe inspiring view of the mountains facing east and a bench to rest weary little legs.”

Photo by Rachel Sowards Thompson

Credit.value: #mypubliclandsroadtrip 2016: Get outdoors Baby, King Range National Conservation Area

184953594.title: File:Balcon del Diablo, Landscape view of Yuncaypata Valley, February 2026 40.jpg

ObjectName.value: Balcon del Diablo, Landscape view of Yuncaypata Valley, February 2026 40

Categories.value: Self-published work|Files with coordinates missing SDC location of creation|Balcón del diablo

ImageDescription.value:
View of the Balcon del Diablo archeological site located on the right bank of the Chakan River.

It can be seen in the pictures, the majestic landscape surrounded the Balcon del Diablo which is a natural rock formation located in the archeological site of Chakan placed on the outskirts of Cusco. this gigantic limestone cliff is get through with the Chakan river, creating a natural bridge due to the erosion generated along time the riverbed. Below this natural caveland it observed on its ceiling a big rift on the limestone also inside this cave land some people left tiny Apacheta to a hallmark for every voyager who passed beneath this natural bridge. This cave land has a length of 45 meter long inside contains several mound of stone which are the Apachetas, this practice came fron the Andean culture that is a symbolic structure make with stones around or in this case inside the natural bridge. the Apacheta is building such a offering to the Apus, also requirement to the Andean deities protection for hikers and travelers asking for a safe journey, strength and protection on the trail. once people got through the cave land of the Balcon del Diablo, we can observe a mystic carved stone steps, this pieces of art it called the Chakana which is perfectly hewn on the limestone also well polished, alongside this Chakana is located the Inka wall that connect directly with the Andean wall. Walking few steps to the Balcon del Diablo on the right side of the Balcon del Diablo is a natural window which the town people called the Balcon del Diablo due the high altitude is placed inside the massive bedrock. this balcony has a triangular shape and local people left some inscriptions on the rock

Note: people usually cross this natural bridge on barefoot.

Credit.value: Own work

Categories.value: Canis latrans lestes|Bureau of Land Management areas in Wyoming|Flickr images reviewed by FlickreviewR 2|Canis latrans in Wyoming|Mammals on slopes|Side views of coyotes|Walking coyotes|Coyotes looking at viewer

ImageDescription.value:
The Alkali Draw WSA encompasses 16,990 acres of BLM-administered land and 640 acres of state land. The study area includes a portion of the Red Desert Area. Alkali Draw in the main drainage running eastwardly from the Bush Rim and Steamboat Mountain. A series of smaller draws creates a washboard topographic effect. Big sagebrush and grease wood are the principle vegetative species.

This area offers primitive and unconfined recreation such as hiking, horseback riding, camping, photography and sightseeing. Some small caves are found in the area and offer opportunity for recreation. The rims and cliff escarpments provide some non-technical climbing opportunities and challenging hikes. This is a fee-free area. Portions of the boundary road area ADA accessible.

BLM photo by Jo Foster.

LATITUDE/LONGITUDE 42.068423 / -108.830291

DIRECTIONS State Highway 28 east from Farson 15 miles turn south on county road 4-21. In approximately 25 miles the county road will become the north

96478640.title: File:Grand Canyon National Park Bright Angel Trail - Sunset 0162 (6924462211).jpg

ObjectName.value: Grand Canyon National Park Bright Angel Trail - Sunset 0162 (6924462211)

Categories.value: Hiking|Bright Angel Trail|Files with coordinates missing SDC location of creation|Flickr images reviewed by FlickreviewR 2|Files from Grand Canyon NPS Flickr stream

ImageDescription.value:
The final rays of sunset illuminate Zoroaster, Brahma and Deva Temples as a day hiker approaches the Second Tunnel, during an ascent of the Bright Angel Trail in Grand Canyon National Park. At this point on the trail, hikers are walking on the edge of the Bright Angel Fault. The trail was constructed down this natural break in the rock layers where the rocks on one side are uplifted 189 feet (58 m) higher than on the other. Today’s Bright Angel Trail approximates a route used for millennia by the many Native American groups that have called the Grand Canyon home.

Since the Bright Angel Trail starts into the canyon from Grand Canyon Village, it is the park’s most popular hiking trail. Maintained, graded for stock, with regular drinking water and covered rest-houses, it is without question the safest trail in Grand Canyon National Park. There is a ranger station located at the trail’s halfway point (Indian Garden) and one at the bottom of the canyon (Bright Angel Campground). Visitors hiking for the first time at Grand Canyon often use this trail in conjunction with the South Kaibab Trail. Particularly during hot weather, it makes sense to ascend via the Bright Angel Trail because of potable water, regular shade, emergency phones, and the ranger presence. NPS photo by Michael Quinn

Read the complete trail description here: <a href="http://www.nps.gov/grca/planyourvisit/upload/Bright_Angel_Trail.pdf" rel="nofollow">www.nps.gov/grca/planyourvisit/upload/Bright_Angel_Trail.pdf</a>

ImageDescription.value:
PR 1 mountain hiking trail – Vereda do Arieiro / Vereda do Areeiro between Pico do Areeiro and Pico Ruivo on Madeira Island, Portugal, on 20 August 2022.

The photograph shows a stone section of a narrow path running along a ridge in the central mountain massif of Madeira. The frame includes a hiker with a backpack walking down stone steps, metal posts and safety cables along the trail, rocky slopes, sharp mountain formations, scree, mountain vegetation and deeply cut valleys.

The image documents mountain hiking in Madeira, the exposed character and safety infrastructure of the PR 1 trail, the volcanic mountain landscape of the island and the protected central mountain massif of Madeira.
